div.head: Grið 1
div.ab: Godes grið is ealra griða selast to geearnianne ⁊ geornost to healdanne ⁊ þær nehst þæs cynges.
Godes grið is ealra griða selast to geearnianne and geornost to healdanne, and þær nehst, þæs cynges.
Gottes Friedensschutz ist unter allen Sonderfrieden am vorzüglichsten zu verdienen und am eifrigsten zu halten; und demnächst [der] des Königs.
God's peace-protection is, of all special peaces, the most excellent to earn and the most zealously to be kept; and next to it [that] of the king.
Of all forms of sanctuary, the sanctuary of God is the best to deserve and the most diligently to be held, and next to that, the king’s.

div.note: Liebermann compares I Cn 2.1.; T: corrected against Rabin, DOML 66 (2020), p. 22 (before: ‘Godes grið is ealra griða selast to geearnianne and geornost to healdanne and þær nehst þæs cynges.’); AZ: corrected against Rabin p. 22 / 23, October 2026 (was “∅; is; iii; iii; iii; ix; ix; ix; 3– 5 The nostalgic tone of clauses 3 through 5 recalls the similar evocation of an idealized past in the opening clauses of the first item in The Compilation on Status, On the Ranks of People and Law, a text likely composed at approximately the same time as this one. It also highlights the present-day deterioration in ecclesiastical status, which made necessary the injunctions that follow.”, now “|; is,; III; III; III; IX; IX; IX; ∅”); V: page of the modern editor’s text / translation, checked against Rabin (translation on the facing page), October 2026 (e.g. was “22”, now “22 / 23”; 38 rows of Grið)
Manuscripts: G = London, British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i, fol. 92v–95v.
the sanctuary of God: Godes grið is a favorite phrase of Wulfstan’s and survives almost exclusively in his writings.

the king’s: The extent of the king’s sanctuary is defined in the short tenth-century legal tract Pax, which reads in its entirety, “Thus far shall be the king’s sanctuary from the city gate, where he is sitting, in four directions, that is, three miles and three furlongs and three lineal acres and nine feet and nine handspans and nine barleycorns” (Ðus feor sceal beon þæs cinges grið fram his burhgeate, þær he is sittende, on feower healfe his, ðæt is III mila and III furlang and III æcera bræde and IX fota and IX scæftamunda and IX berecorna). The mention of the king sitting at the city gate refers to the practice of holding court at a town’s gate. For an early reference to this practice, see Deuteronomy 21:18–21.
